lessons.title: Mechanical Dewatering: Centrifuges and Presses
lessons.body:
After you extract starch from cassava, you have a thin slurryâabout 95% water. You must remove most of that water before drying. Mechanical dewatering does this fast and cheaply. The two main tools are the centrifuge and the screw press.

A centrifuge spins the slurry at high speed. The starch, being heavier, settles to the outside, while water stays in the middle. You can use a simple basket centrifugeâa perforated drum lined with filter cloth. Pour in slurry, spin for 5â10 minutes at 1,500â3,000 RPM. The water flies out, leaving a moist starch cake with about 40â50% moisture. For small-scale, a manual or motorized basket centrifuge costs $300â$800. In Nigeria, many processors use locally fabricated stainless steel centrifuges.

A screw press (also called a dewatering press) works continuously. Slurry enters one end, and a rotating screw pushes it against a cone or plate. Water squeezes out through screens, and dry cake exits the other end. A good screw press can reduce moisture to 50â60%. These are common in Ghana and Tanzania for cassava starch. You can build a small screw press with a 2 HP motor and stainless steel parts for about $500.

If you lack machinery, you can use a hydraulic press or even a manual jack press. Fill filter cloth bags with slurry, stack them, and press for 30â60 minutes. This gets moisture down to 55â65%. Itâs labour-intensive but works for 50â100 kg batches.

Key tips: Always use clean water and stainless steel or plastic equipment to avoid darkening. Add a little salt (0.1%) to help water release. After dewatering, break the cake into small crumblesâthis speeds up drying. Never let the cake sit wet for more than 12 hours, or it will ferment and smell. For best results, aim for 50â60% moisture before drying. This cuts drying time by half compared to drying slurry directly.

lessons.title: Solar Drying of Cassava Starch
lessons.body:
Solar drying is the cheapest way to dry cassava starch in Africa. You use the sunâs heat and moving air to evaporate water. But open sun drying on mats or concrete is risky: dust, rain, insects, and animals can contaminate your starch. A simple solar dryer solves this.

Build a solar cabinet dryer. Make a wooden or metal box 2 m long, 1 m wide, and 0.5 m deep. Cover the top with clear polythene or glass. Paint the inside black. Add vents at the bottom and top for airflow. Inside, place trays of starch crumbles 2â3 cm thick. The sun heats the air, which rises and exits, carrying moisture. Temperature inside reaches 40â60Â°C. Drying takes 1â2 days in bright sunshine.

A more efficient design is the solar tunnel dryer. Itâs a long hoop structure covered with UV-resistant plastic. A small fan (12V, 10W) at one end pushes air through. You can dry 50â100 kg of starch per batch in 8â12 hours. Cost: $200â$500. In Kenya, such dryers are used for cassava and other crops.

For best results: Spread starch no thicker than 2 cm. Stir every 2 hours with a clean wooden rake. Start drying early (8 AM) to catch maximum sun. Bring trays inside at night to avoid dew. If humidity is high, add a small charcoal stove or electric heater at the air inletâbut keep it outside the drying chamber to avoid smoke.

Solar drying works best in dry seasons. In rainy months, you need backup. A hybrid solar-gas or solar-electric dryer costs more but ensures production. Always use food-grade plastic or stainless steel trays. Never dry on bare ground or on tarpaulin that may leach chemicals. With a good solar dryer, you can reach 12â14% moisture in 1â2 sunny days, ready for milling or packaging.

lessons.title: Hot Air Drying Systems
lessons.body:
When you need to dry starch fast or during rainy season, hot air drying is the answer. You burn fuel (gas, diesel, firewood, or biomass) to heat air, then blow it over the starch. The hot air picks up moisture and exits. This works 24/7 and gives consistent results.

A simple hot air dryer is a cabinet with trays and a heat source. You can use a gas burner (LPG) or a diesel furnace. A fan (0.5â2 HP) blows air through a heat exchanger, then into the drying chamber. Temperature should be 50â70Â°C. Higher temperatures can gelatinize starch, making it sticky and hard to dry. Airflow must be strong enough to move moisture outâabout 5â10 mÂ³ per minute per 100 kg of wet starch.

For small-scale, a rotary dryer is better. Itâs a long cylinder that turns slowly. Hot air flows through, and starch tumbles, exposing new surfaces. You can dry 200â500 kg per hour. These are common in medium-scale cassava processing in Nigeria and Thailand. A used rotary dryer might cost $2,000â$5,000.

If you have a biomass furnace, you can burn cassava peels, rice husks, or wood chips. This cuts fuel costs. But never let smoke touch the starchâuse a heat exchanger. In Tanzania, some processors use a furnace with a stainless steel pipe to heat air, keeping smoke separate.

Key controls: Measure temperature with a thermometer. Keep it below 70Â°C. Check moisture every 30 minutes. Stop when starch reaches 12â14% moisture. Over-drying wastes fuel and makes starch dusty. Under-drying causes mould. Clean the dryer dailyâstarch dust can explode if it builds up near a flame. With good hot air drying, you can process year-round and meet large orders.

lessons.title: Monitoring Moisture Content
lessons.body:
You cannot guess when starch is dry. Too wet (above 14% moisture) and it will mould in storage. Too dry (below 10%) and you lose weight and money. You must measure moisture accurately.

The best tool is a moisture meter. A handheld grain moisture meter works for starch. Cost: $50â$200. You fill a small cup with starch, press a button, and read the percentage. Calibrate it monthly with a known sample. If you canât afford a meter, use the salt test. Put 10 g of starch in a dry bottle with 10 g of dry salt. Shake for 1 minute. If salt sticks to the sides, starch is too wet (above 14%). If salt stays loose, itâs dry enough.

Another method: the squeeze test. Take a handful of starch and squeeze. If it holds shape and feels damp, itâs above 15%. If it crumbles and feels dry, itâs around 12â14%. This is not precise but works in the field.

For accurate results, use the oven method. Weigh 10 g of starch in a metal dish. Dry in an oven at 130Â°C for 1 hour. Cool in a desiccator and weigh again. Moisture % = (initial weight â final weight) / initial weight Ã 100. This is the standard lab method.

During drying, test every 30â60 minutes. Record the weight loss. For a 100 kg batch, you know you need to remove about 85 kg of water to go from 85% moisture (slurry) to 12% moisture (dry starch). But after dewatering, you start at 50% moisture, so you need to remove about 38 kg of water per 100 kg. Track your progress.

Store dried starch in clean, dry sacks. Keep a sample from each batch and test it weekly for the first month. If moisture rises, your storage is damp. Move to a dry room. Always aim for 12â13% moisture for long-term storage.

lessons.title: Preventing Contamination During Drying
lessons.body:
Drying is when your starch is most vulnerable. Dust, insects, rodents, and dirty hands can ruin a whole batch. Contaminated starch fails food safety tests, sells for less, or gets rejected. You must keep it clean.

First, location. Never dry starch near animal pens, toilets, or garbage. Build your dryer at least 20 m from these. If using open sun, dry on raised tables covered with food-grade mesh. Never dry on bare ground, tarpaulin, or concrete that has been used for chemicals. Use stainless steel or food-grade plastic trays.

Second, protect from insects and birds. Cover solar dryers with fine mesh (0.5 mm) at air inlets and outlets. For open drying, use a mesh tent or a simple frame with mosquito netting. Fruit flies and beetles love starch. A single fly can lay eggs that hatch into maggots. If you see small holes or webbing, discard that batch.

Third, human hygiene. Workers must wash hands with soap before touching starch. Wear clean aprons and hairnets. No eating, smoking, or spitting near the dryer. Sick workers should stay away. Use clean toolsâwooden rakes and shovels dedicated to starch only. Never use the same shovel for manure or waste.

Fourth, control dust. Starch dust floats and settles on everything. Keep the drying area swept. But donât use a broom that sheds bristles. Use a damp cloth or a vacuum. If dust builds up in a hot air dryer, it can explode. Clean the dryer after every batch.

Fifth, water quality. If you rewet starch (e.g., to adjust moisture), use only clean, potable water. Never use river water or well water that might contain bacteria. After drying, cool starch completely before packing. Pack in new, clean polypropylene sacks. Store on pallets, not on the floor. With these steps, your starch will be clean, safe, and ready for market.

lessons.title: Energy Efficiency in Drying
lessons.body:
Drying uses a lot of energyâwhether sun, gas, or electricity. In Africa, energy is expensive or unreliable. Saving energy means more profit. Hereâs how.

First, dewater mechanically as much as possible. Removing 1 kg of water by pressing costs about 10 times less than removing it by drying. So invest in a good press or centrifuge. Aim for 50% moisture before drying. This cuts drying energy by half.

Second, insulate your dryer. For hot air dryers, wrap the chamber with fibreglass or rockwool insulation. A well-insulated dryer loses less heat. You can save 20â30% on fuel. Seal all gaps. Use a door that closes tightly. For solar dryers, add a black absorber plate and double glazing to trap more heat.

Third, reuse heat. Exhaust air from a hot air dryer is still warm (40â50Â°C) and humid. Use a heat exchanger to preheat incoming air. This recovers 30â50% of heat. Simple systems use a pipe-in-pipe exchanger. In Kenya, some processors use this on cassava dryers.

Fourth, control airflow. Too much air wastes heat; too little air keeps moisture in. Use a variable speed fan or a damper. Test: if exhaust air feels very humid, increase airflow. If it feels dry and hot, reduce airflow. Aim for 5â10 mÂ³/min per 100 kg wet starch.

Fifth, use renewable energy. Solar is free after installation. For hot air, consider biogas from cassava waste. A small biogas digester (2â5 mÂ³) can produce enough gas to run a dryer for 2â3 hours per day. In Nigeria, some processors use biogas from peels. Also, burn agricultural residues (rice husks, maize cobs) in a gasifier to produce heat. This is cheaper than diesel.

Sixth, schedule drying during sunny hours. If you have both solar and backup, use solar first. Only run the hot air dryer when needed. Keep records of fuel use per batch. Aim to reduce by 10% each month. With these practices, you can cut drying costs by 40â60%.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of mechanical dewatering in cassava starch processing?
options: A) To remove most of the water before drying
B) To add moisture to the starch
quiz.explanation: Mechanical dewatering removes water quickly and cheaply, reducing the load on dryers.

quiz.q: Which machine uses high-speed spinning to separate water from starch?
quiz.explanation: A centrifuge spins slurry, causing denser starch to settle while water is flung out.

quiz.q: After mechanical dewatering, what is the typical moisture content of the starch cake?
quiz.explanation: Dewatering reduces moisture from about 95% to 40â60%, depending on the method.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of a screw press over a batch centrifuge?
options: C) It dries the starch completely
quiz.explanation: A screw press processes slurry continuously, making it suitable for larger volumes.

quiz.q: Why should you break dewatered starch cake into crumbles before drying?
options: A) To make it look better
quiz.explanation: Smaller pieces expose more surface area, allowing faster moisture evaporation.

quiz.q: What is a major risk of open sun drying on mats or concrete?
options: B) Contamination from dust, insects, and animals
quiz.explanation: Open drying exposes starch to dirt, pests, and weather, compromising quality.

quiz.q: In a solar cabinet dryer, what colour should the inside be painted and why?
quiz.explanation: Black surfaces absorb more solar radiation, raising the internal temperature.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness for spreading starch in a solar dryer?
quiz.explanation: A 2â3 cm layer allows air to circulate and moisture to escape efficiently.

quiz.q: Why should you bring solar drying trays inside at night?
options: B) To prevent dew and moisture reabsorption
quiz.explanation: Night dew can add moisture back to the starch, undoing drying progress.

quiz.q: What is a solar tunnel dryer?
options: A) A small box with a glass lid
B) A long hoop structure covered with plastic and a fan
C) A concrete floor with black paint
quiz.explanation: A solar tunnel dryer uses a long covered structure and forced air for faster drying.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for hot air drying of cassava starch?
quiz.explanation: Temperatures above 70Â°C can gelatinize starch, so 50â70Â°C is safe and effective.

quiz.q: What happens if hot air drying temperature exceeds 70Â°C?
options: A) Starch dries faster and better
B) Starch may gelatinize and become sticky
quiz.explanation: High heat causes starch granules to swell and gelatinize, making drying difficult.

quiz.q: In a rotary dryer, how is starch dried?
options: A) It is pressed between rollers
B) It tumbles in a rotating cylinder with hot air
D) It is soaked in hot water
quiz.explanation: A rotary dryer turns slowly, tumbling starch to expose new surfaces to hot air.

quiz.q: Why should smoke never touch the starch in a biomass hot air dryer?
options: B) Smoke contaminates starch with harmful chemicals and odour
quiz.explanation: Smoke contains tar and carcinogens that make starch unsafe and unpalatable.

quiz.q: What is a sign that starch is over-dried?
options: B) It becomes very dusty and light
quiz.explanation: Over-drying removes too much moisture, making starch dusty and reducing yield.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture content for dried cassava starch for safe storage?
quiz.explanation: 12â14% moisture prevents mould growth while avoiding excessive weight loss.

quiz.q: Which tool gives the most accurate moisture reading?
quiz.explanation: A calibrated moisture meter provides precise percentage readings, unlike field tests.

quiz.q: How does the salt test indicate if starch is too wet?
options: B) Salt sticks to the bottle sides
quiz.explanation: If starch is above 14% moisture, salt clumps and sticks due to dampness.

quiz.q: In the oven method, what temperature is used to dry a starch sample?
quiz.explanation: 130Â°C for 1 hour drives off all moisture without burning the starch.

quiz.q: Why should you record weight loss during drying?
options: A) To know when to stop and ensure consistent moisture
quiz.explanation: Tracking weight loss helps determine when the target moisture content is reached.

quiz.q: What is a major source of contamination during drying?
options: B) Dirty hands and unclean tools
quiz.explanation: Workers and tools can introduce bacteria, dirt, and pests if not properly cleaned.

quiz.q: How far should a drying area be from animal pens or toilets?
quiz.explanation: A 20 m buffer reduces risks from flies, dust, and odours that can contaminate starch.

quiz.q: Why is fine mesh used on solar dryers?
options: B) To keep insects and birds out
quiz.explanation: Mesh allows air but prevents pests from reaching the starch.

quiz.q: What should workers wear when handling drying starch?
quiz.explanation: Clean aprons and hairnets prevent hair and dirt from contaminating the starch.

quiz.q: Why is starch dust dangerous in a hot air dryer?
options: A) It can explode if ignited
quiz.explanation: Starch dust is combustible; in high concentrations near a flame, it can explode.

quiz.q: How can you save energy by mechanical dewatering?
options: A) It removes water cheaply, reducing drying load
B) It adds heat to the starch
quiz.explanation: Removing water mechanically costs far less than evaporating it with heat.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of insulating a hot air dryer?
options: A) It makes the dryer heavier
B) It reduces heat loss and saves fuel
quiz.explanation: Insulation keeps heat inside, lowering fuel consumption by 20â30%.

quiz.q: How can you reuse heat from exhaust air?
options: A) By using a heat exchanger to preheat incoming air
B) By blowing it directly on starch
C) By storing it in a tank
D) By mixing it with cold water
quiz.explanation: A heat exchanger transfers warmth from exhaust to fresh air, recovering energy.

quiz.q: What is a renewable energy option for hot air drying?
quiz.explanation: Biogas produced from cassava peels is a cheap, renewable fuel for dryers.

quiz.q: What should you do if exhaust air from a dryer feels very humid?
quiz.explanation: High humidity in exhaust means air is saturated; increasing airflow removes moisture faster.
